content: Hydroxyzine, when administered orally, is indicated for the symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension associated with psychoneurosis. It can also be used as an adjunct in organic disease states where anxiety is present. Additionally, it is effective in managing pruritus caused by allergic conditions such as chronic urticaria, atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, and other histamine-mediated pruritic conditions. Hydroxyzine serves as a sedative when used as premedication or following general anesthesia. It has the potential to enhance the effects of meperidine (Demerol®) and barbiturates, necessitating individualized adjustments in pre-anesthetic adjunctive therapy. However, it does not affect the action of atropine or other belladonna alkaloids. Hydroxyzine is also compatible with digitalis and can be used concurrently without interference. The long-term efficacy of hydroxyzine as an antianxiety agent, defined as use beyond four months, has not been systematically evaluated in clinical studies. Physicians are advised to periodically reassess the drug's utility for each patient. Dosage Guidelines: 1. For anxiety and tension associated with psychoneurosis or as an adjunct in organic disease states: Adults: 50-100 mg four times daily (q.i.d.). Children under 6 years: 50 mg daily in divided doses. Children over 6 years: 50-100 mg daily in divided doses. 2. For pruritus due to allergic conditions or histamine-mediated pruritus: Adults: 25 mg three to four times daily (t.i.d. or q.i.d.). Children under 6 years: 50 mg daily in divided doses. Children over 6 years: 50-100 mg daily in divided doses. 3. As a sedative for premedication or post-anesthesia: Adults: 50-100 mg. Children: 0.6 mg/kg. When treatment begins via intramuscular administration, subsequent doses may be given orally. Dosages should always be adjusted based on the patient’s therapeutic response. Pregnancy and Nursing Considerations: Hydroxyzine has been shown to cause fetal abnormalities in animal studies (rats and mice) at doses significantly higher than the human therapeutic range. There is insufficient clinical data to confirm its safety during early pregnancy. Therefore, hydroxyzine is contraindicated in early pregnancy. It is also unknown whether hydroxyzine is excreted in human breast milk, so it should not be administered to nursing mothers. Adverse Effects: 1. Anticholinergic Effects: Dry mouth. 2. Central Nervous System Effects: Drowsiness, which is usually transient and may resolve with continued therapy or dose reduction. Rare cases of involuntary motor activity, including tremors and convulsions, typically at doses much higher than recommended. Clinically significant respiratory depression has not been observed at recommended doses. Special Considerations for the Elderly: Elderly patients are more likely to have reduced renal function, necessitating careful dose selection. Sedating drugs, including hydroxyzine, may cause confusion and over-sedation in this population. It is recommended to start elderly patients on lower doses and monitor them closely. Overdose Management: If an overdose occurs and vomiting has not occurred spontaneously, it should be induced. Gastric lavage is recommended. Supportive care, including frequent monitoring of vital signs and close observation, is essential. Hypotension, if present, can be managed with intravenous fluids and agents such as Levophed® (levarterenol) or Aramine® (metaraminol). Epinephrine should not be used, as hydroxyzine counteracts its pressor effects. There is no specific antidote for hydroxyzine overdose, and hemodialysis is unlikely to be beneficial unless other substances, such as barbiturates, have been co-ingested. Formulation Details: Each 5 mL (teaspoon) of the oral solution contains 10 mg of hydroxyzine hydrochloride. Inactive ingredients include alcohol (0.5% v/v), corn syrup, methylparaben, peppermint flavor, propylene glycol, purified water, sodium benzoate, and sucrose. Sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid may be used to adjust the pH as needed. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride has been associated with fixed drug eruptions in post-marketing reports.
